steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper presenting RTS-GT, a dataset with ground truth trajectories from robotic total stations. Cover how ground truth is usually produced for SLAM datasets and its limits, what robotic total stations offer, and what our dataset provides.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Ground truth for SLAM datasets: indoor and outdoor practice, and limits
- Robotic total stations (RTS) as a reference: how they work, prisms, current limitations
- Uncertainty of ground truth
- Motivation and the RTS-GT dataset

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Ground truth trajectories that are accurate and precise are essential in open-source datasets to evaluate SLAM algorithms. Motion capture systems like Vicon or OptiTrack have become the de facto standard to generate this ground truth indoors. But they cannot be deployed outside, because direct sunlight corrupts the readings and much larger areas need to be covered. For outdoor deployments, most datasets use GNSS in RTK mode integrated with an INS to compute the reference trajectories with an accuracy of several centimeters. However, these localization systems are vulnerable to GNSS outages, which can be seen on the KITTI dataset. A few datasets use HD maps from a terrestrial laser scanner to get the reference within centimeter accuracy. But surveying is still an open challenge, especially in off-road terrain where there are few reference planes, which makes it hard to align scans.

In recent years a limited number of datasets used a single RTS to generate these references indoors or outdoors with different platforms. An RTS is a surveying instrument that can measure the position of a reflective target (from now on, prism) with millimeter precision, and it has two modes: 1) static, when the prism is fixed, and 2) dynamic, when the prism is moving. There are also two types of prism, active and passive. An active prism has LEDs that emit a unique infrared signature, and this signature lets multiple RTS automatically track different prisms in their field of view. Even with its accuracy and robustness, a single RTS can only give the reference 3D position of the platform it tracks. This is because only one prism can be tracked while the robot is moving. With three passive prisms you can get the six-DOF reference trajectory by collecting the data manually while the robot is static, but this makes data collection cumbersome. As far as we know, active prisms were never used in any released dataset that provides six-DOF reference trajectories generated by RTS in dynamic mode. Also, recent research makes it possible to estimate the uncertainty for a multi-RTS setup. This uncertainty on the ground truth is not available in state-of-the-art SLAM datasets, which can lead to unbiased comparisons since many SLAM algorithms are getting close to centimeter-level accuracy.

The main motivation of this work is to provide a high-quality dataset that covers a variety of challenging environments and that further motivates ground truth generation for SLAM algorithms. Our previous research showed that generating reliable six-DOF reference trajectories of a moving robot with three RTS is now feasible. Following up on this, we present RTS-GT, a dataset that provides six-DOF reference trajectories from two different types of setup, three RTS and three GNSS receivers. The RTS-GT dataset was collected over 17 months in diverse weather conditions, and the trajectories total over 49 kilometers. With this dataset we provide and compare the precision and the reproducibility of the setups in multiple weather conditions and in different environments, as shown in Figure 1, and this shows that RTS are more reliable than GNSS to generate ground truth trajectories.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Accurate and precise ground truth trajectories in open-source datasets are essential to evaluate SLAM algorithms [1]. Motion capture systems such as Vicon or OptiTrack have become the de facto standard to generate such ground truth in indoor environments [2]. However, they are not suitable for deployment outside, due to direct sunlight corrupting the readings and the need to cover much larger areas. For outdoor deployments, most datasets use GNSS in RTK mode integrated with INS to compute the reference trajectories within several centimeters accuracy [3,4,5]. Meanwhile, such localization systems are vulnerable to GNSS outages, as seen on the KITTI dataset [6]. A few datasets rely on HD maps from a terrestrial laser scanner to obtain the reference within centimeter accuracy [7,8]. However, surveying remains an open challenge, especially in off-road terrain where reference planes are scarce, which makes it hard to align scans.

In recent years, a limited number of datasets used a single RTS to generate such references indoors or outdoors with various platforms [9,10]. An RTS is a surveying instrument capable of measuring the position of a reflective target (hereafter prism) with millimeter precision in two modes: 1) static, when the prism is fixed, and 2) dynamic, when the prism is in motion. Moreover, two types of prism exist, active and passive. An active prism is equipped with LEDs that emit a unique infrared signature, which enables multiple RTS to automatically track different prisms within their field of view. Despite their accuracy and robustness, a single RTS can only provide the reference 3D position of the tracked platform, since only one prism can be tracked while the robot is in motion. Using three passive prisms, it is possible to obtain the six-DOF reference trajectory by manually collecting the data when the robot is static [11], which makes data collection cumbersome. To the best of our knowledge, active prisms were never used in any released dataset providing six-DOF reference trajectories generated by RTS in dynamic mode. Moreover, recent research enables estimating the uncertainty of a multi-RTS setup [12]. This uncertainty on ground truth is not available in state-of-the-art SLAM datasets, which can lead to unbiased comparisons as many SLAM algorithms are approaching centimeter-level accuracy [13].

The key motivation for this work is to provide a high-quality dataset that covers a variety of challenging environments and further motivates ground truth generation for SLAM algorithms. As shown in our previous research [14,12], generating reliable six-DOF reference trajectories of a moving robot with three RTS is now feasible. As a follow-up, we present RTS-GT, a dataset providing six-DOF reference trajectories from two different types of setup, three RTS and three GNSS receivers. The RTS-GT dataset was collected over 17 months in diverse weather conditions, totaling over 49 kilometers of trajectories. With this dataset, we provide and compare the precision and reproducibility of the setups in multiple weather conditions and different environments, as shown in Figure 1, demonstrating that RTS are more reliable than GNSS for generating ground truth trajectories.
